name: Rafael Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Rafael. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a respiratory ward, so COPD, pneumonia, people on oxygen or on those breathing masks we call NIV. A shift is obs, sats, nebulisers, blood gases, and a lot of helping breathless people to the toilet slowly. I like the technical side, the machines, the numbers. What wears me out is the lifting, and that I still need a senior to check my blood gas readings.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents in the flat above their takeaway on Station Road. I help out there on my days off sometimes. I've got about five months of savings, and I use AI every day, for everything from my revision to helping my dad with his menu and accounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. I'd be a bit disappointed, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI was oversold, but the tools are still useful if you know how to use them. I'd probably post a few tips on how nurses can use it for revision. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't change much. Living with my parents at twenty-seven isn't glamorous, but it means every spare pound goes toward my own home-care business one day. The ward is short-staffed, so my job's secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. Finish my respiratory competencies, keep saving, keep helping my dad. Use AI for my revision. Maybe look at agency shifts for extra money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the home-care business idea.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lots of older people want to stay at home after hospital. A small agency with good nurses could do well. I've seen how badly discharge planning goes. It's a few years off, but I think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your dad think of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He loves it. He started the takeaway from nothing. He says the hardest part is the first year, and to save more than I think I need.

think: Living with my parents means every pound goes toward **my business** one day.
The ward is **short-staffed**, so my job is secure.
do: Keep **saving** and helping my dad at the takeaway.
Look at **agency shifts** for extra money.

steps.text: Finish his respiratory competencies on the ward

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing, booking, planning. That's the admin side of any care business too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an opportunity for nurses who are willing to learn. Complaining won't help. I'd encourage colleagues to try the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's good for me. Hospitals buy software slowly, so a nurse who learns these tools now gets a few years' head start on everyone else. And for a future care business, AI could do the rota and invoicing, which cuts costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the ward's go-to for the new system. I'd start a short business course online in the evenings. I'd keep saving and maybe pick up agency shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The admin staff. And some of the older nurses who hate computers. I'd try to help them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is it all upside for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. The risk is that bigger care firms use AI too and squeeze out small ones before I start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Then robots three years after. That's fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to take charge of their own futures and not wait for the government. Learn, save, build something. I'd say it on my socials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, if robots can do hands-on care by 2031, I'd rather be the man who owns the robots than the nurse they replace. But I'm a junior with five months' savings. Starting a business that fast is a big risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a small home-care agency in 2027, using AI for scheduling and billing, with a couple of nurses. Keep my hospital job part-time as a backup. I'd save every spare pound and ask my dad to help with the start-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited too, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the nurses you'd hire when robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep them as long as people want people. Maybe they'd supervise the robots. I don't have all the answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My car. I'd use my dad's van. And the gym. Everything into the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's more realistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same: take charge, learn, build. With five years there's no excuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is long enough to start a small home-care firm with real nurses and add robots when they're ready. I'd have experience by 2031 and robots would come around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my competencies, do the business course, start the agency in 2028 with a couple of nurses. Use AI for admin. Keep saving and keep working agency shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. There's time to build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could stop you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Regulation. Care agencies have a lot of rules. I'd need to learn them properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your parents be part of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would do the books, he loves numbers. My mum would make sure everyone was fed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so people should prepare: learn, save, build. Don't wait for handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is time to build a business properly, with my dad's advice and my own savings, not a government grant. By 2036 I'd have a decade of nursing behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get experienced on the ward, do the business course, start the agency around 2030. Use AI throughout. Buy robots when they're ready, around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new nurse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the tools early and think like a business owner, even if you never become one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that worries you, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents getting older. I'd want to look after them, and the takeaway won't run forever.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have to start a business before I'm ready, with not much money, and that's a lot of risk. What would help is simpler rules for starting a care agency and banks willing to lend to nurses who want to build something.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I've learned on the ward. The ward taught me that a frightened old man calms down when someone holds his hand, and no business plan should forget that.

He lives with his parents above their **takeaway**, saving about five months of costs.
He's **traditional and pro-business**, preferring self-reliance over government help.
He sees AI and robots as a chance to build a **home-care agency**.
He turns **anxious** only in the fastest picture, where he'd have to start before he's ready.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have to start a business too early with little money.

**Banks willing to lend** to nurses starting businesses.
